objectives: Master cinema lens fundamentals: focal length, aperture, depth of field, anamorphic.
Compare film vs digital cameras + understand sensors + recording formats.
Reason about resolution + frame rate trade-offs in modern production.

slides.title: Cinema lenses: focal length, aperture, depth of field, anamorphic
slides.body:
**Focal length** ($f$, mm) — distance from the optical center of a lens to the sensor when focused at infinity. Sets **angle of view**. On a Super 35 (~24 × 13.5 mm) sensor:
- 18 mm: ultrawide (~85° horizontal). Wide-angle lensing — distortion + immersive — Lubezki / Cuarón.
- 25-35 mm: wide-normal. 'Documentary' feel.
- 50 mm: normal — close to human perspective.
- 75-100 mm: medium telephoto — flattering portrait.
- 135-300 mm: telephoto — sport, isolation, sniper POV.

**Aperture** ($f$-number, $N = f/D$, where $D$ is the entrance-pupil diameter). Common stops: f/1.4 → f/2 → f/2.8 → f/4 → f/5.6 → f/8 → f/11 → f/16 — each step halves the light. Smaller $N$ = more light + shallower depth of field.

**T-stop** = transmission stop — measured rather than calculated $f$-stop. Cinema lenses are rated in T-stops (typically T1.3-T2.8 wide open) to guarantee photometric consistency across the set: a 50 mm T2.0 + a 100 mm T2.0 expose identically. Still-photo $f$-stops (geometric) can differ by 1/3 stop from their true transmission.

**Depth of field** (DoF) — range of distances appearing acceptably sharp.

$$\text{DoF} \approx \frac{2 \, N \, c \, u^2}{f^2}$$

where $u$ = subject distance, $c$ = circle of confusion (~0.025 mm for Super 35). Shallow DoF (low $N$, long $f$, close $u$) isolates subject — the classical 50 mm T1.3 close-up. Deep focus (large $N$, short $f$, distant $u$) — Toland-style.

**Bokeh** — aesthetic of out-of-focus highlights. Determined by aperture-blade count + shape + lens design. Round + creamy (Zeiss Master Prime) vs oval (anamorphic) vs swirly (vintage Petzval).

**Lens history + manufacturers**:
- **Petzval** (Joseph Petzval, 1840) — first calculated photographic lens. Fast for its day; characteristic swirly bokeh.
- **Cooke Optics** (UK, 1893+) — the **Cooke Triplet** (Harold Dennis Taylor, 1893) launched modern photographic optics. Modern cinema lines: **Cooke S4/i**, **S7/i**, **S8/i**, **Anamorphic/i**, **SF (Special Flair)**, **Panchro Classic**. Signature warm 'Cooke look' — slight bloom + warm bias + roll-off in highlights.
- **Carl Zeiss** (Germany) — **Master Prime**, **Ultra Prime**, **Supreme Prime**, **Supreme Radiance**. Clinically sharp, modern, contrasty.
- **Panavision** (US, 1953+) — rental-only. **Primo**, **Primo 70**, **Primo X**, **C-Series Anamorphic**, **G-Series Anamorphic**, **T-Series**, **DXL2**. Panavision's anamorphic optics shape much of Hollywood look.
- **ARRI / Master Anamorphic** + **ARRI Signature Prime** — modern large-format spherical + anamorphic.
- **Angénieux** zooms; **Leica Summilux-C/Summicron-C**.
- **Hawk** + **Vantage One**; **Atlas Orion**; **Tribe7 Blackwing7**; vintage Lomo + Kowa.

**Anamorphic** — squeezes a wider horizontal image onto a 4:3 negative; unsqueezed by projector or in post. Standard squeeze ratio **2× horizontal** → 2.39:1 widescreen from 4:3 capture. Modern **1.3×** + **1.8×** options exist for digital. Anamorphic signatures: **oval bokeh**, **horizontal lens flares** (the blue J. J. Abrams streak), **barrel distortion**, **focus breathing**, **mumps** (face widening at close focus). Spherical lenses produce circular bokeh + neutral distortion. Choosing anamorphic vs spherical is a primary aesthetic decision.

slides.title: Capture: film stocks, digital sensors, recording codecs
slides.body:
**Film origination** — still alive in 2024+:
- **Kodak Vision3 (5219)** — 500T tungsten-balanced color negative; pushable to 1600 ISO; latest Vision3 line (2009+). Vision3 250D, 200T, 50D. *Oppenheimer* (Hoyte van Hoytema, 2023) shot 65 mm + invented IMAX black-and-white Vision3 stock for the film.
- **Fuji Eterna** — discontinued 2013; Kodak now sole major supplier.
- **Format sizes**: 16 mm (Super 16 — 12.5 × 7.4 mm), 35 mm (Super 35 ~ 24 × 13.5 mm), 65 mm (IMAX horizontal 15-perf, 70 mm vertical 5-perf, Panavision Super 70 5-perf).

**Why film survives**: organic grain + highlight roll-off + color science of three emulsions interlocked + emotional + ritual labor. Nolan, P.T. Anderson, Tarantino, Spielberg, Jordan Peele shoot film.

**Digital cinema cameras**:
- **ARRI Alexa** (2010+) — *the* dominant cinema digital camera. Native ISO 800 + LogC3 / LogC4 gamma + ALEV CMOS sensor. **Alexa Mini** (handheld), **Alexa Mini LF** (large-format), **Alexa 35** (2022 — 17 stops dynamic range, REVEAL color science, native ISO 800-6400 dual gain). Most Oscar-winning DPs use Alexa.
- **RED Digital Cinema** (Jim Jannard, 2007+) — pioneered RAW + 4K to 8K cinema digital. **Red One** → **Epic** → **Weapon** → **Helium** → **Monstro** → **V-Raptor** → **V-Raptor XL 8K VV**. R3D codec. Higher resolution + smaller body than Alexa; widely used.
- **Sony Venice / Venice 2** — 8.6K Venice 2 (2021); **Burano** (2024) compact full-frame. X-OCN codec.
- **Panavision DXL2** — Panavision-mounted RED Monstro 8K VV; used on *The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel*, *Snow White*.
- **Blackmagic URSA Cine 12K**, **Canon C700/C500 Mark II**, **Z Cam**, **Kinefinity** — secondary tier.

**Key sensor concepts**:
- **Dynamic range** — stops between noise floor + clipping. Alexa 35 ~17 stops; modern best digital ~14-17; Vision3 negative ~13-14 stops.
- **ISO / native ISO** — sensitivity. Alexa dual-gain at 800/2560 ISO. Pushed ISO trades noise for sensitivity.
- **Log gamma** — encodes 14+ stops into 10/12-bit signal preserving highlight + shadow detail. LogC3 (Alexa), LogC4 (Alexa 35), Sony S-Log3, RED Log3G10, Canon C-Log, Fuji F-Log, Blackmagic Film. Log footage looks flat — viewable LUTs apply contrast + saturation for monitoring.
- **Color science** — proprietary mapping from sensor RAW → log → display. ARRI's color science is widely considered the gold standard.

**Recording codecs**:
- **Apple ProRes** — 422 / 422 HQ / 4444 / 4444 XQ — intra-frame, broadcast standard. ProRes RAW (newer).
- **Avid DNxHR / DNxHD** — equivalent for Avid workflow.
- **ARRIRAW** (.ari) — Alexa native RAW. ProRes 4444 widely used for delivery.
- **R3D (RED RAW)** — RED's wavelet RAW.
- **X-OCN** — Sony's compressed RAW.
- **Blackmagic RAW (BRAW)** — partial-debayer compressed RAW.
- **RAW vs compressed log**: RAW preserves debayer flexibility (white balance, ISO adjustable in post) at large file sizes; log compressed (ProRes/DNxHR) is smaller but locked. Most productions shoot ProRes or R3D for cost + speed.

**File sizes** are massive — 4K ProRes 4444 ~ 1 GB/min; 8K RAW ~ 5+ GB/min. Production data management (DIT, on-set transcoding, LTO archive) is a major cost line.

slides.title: Resolution, frame rate, and HFR experiments
slides.body:
**Resolution**:
- **2K** = 2048 × 1080. DCI standard cinema projection.
- **HD** = 1920 × 1080 (broadcast).
- **UHD / 4K** = 3840 × 2160 (consumer) or 4096 × 2160 (DCI). Default delivery for modern features.
- **6K** = ~6144 × 3240. Common acquisition for 4K delivery (oversampling).
- **8K** = 7680 × 4320 (UHD-2) or 8192 × 4320 (DCI). Sony Venice 2, Red Monstro, ARRI Alexa 65 (6.5K horizontal IMAX).
- **IMAX 70 mm 15-perf** ~ 11K equivalent — still the highest-resolution capture medium in practical use.

**Why shoot higher than you deliver?** Oversampling improves color (Bayer interpolation), reduces aliasing + moiré, enables reframing + stabilization in post.

**Frame rate**:
- **24 fps** — standard cinema since the early sound era. Persistence-of-vision + characteristic 'cinematic motion' (deliberate motion blur at 1/48 s shutter, 180° shutter angle).
- **25 fps** — PAL television (Europe).
- **30 fps** + **29.97 fps** — NTSC television (US legacy).
- **48 fps / 60 fps / 120 fps — HFR (high frame rate)**.

**HFR experiments**:
- **Showscan** (Doug Trumbull, 1980s) — 65 mm at 60 fps. Pioneered HFR theatrical experiment in *Brainstorm* (1983) + theme-park rides. Argued that audience emotional engagement + immersion increased dramatically at 60+ fps.
- **The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey** (Peter Jackson, 2012) — 48 fps + 3D + 4K. Theatrical HFR rollout. Mixed reception — 'looks like video / soap-opera effect.'
- **Billy Lynn's Long Halftime Walk** (Ang Lee, 2016) + **Gemini Man** (2019) — 120 fps + 4K + 3D. Extreme HFR.
- **Avatar: The Way of Water** (Cameron, 2022) — variable frame rate: 48 fps for water scenes, 24 fps for talk scenes. Solved the 'looks like video' problem by reserving HFR for high-motion sequences.
- **High-speed for slow motion** — Phantom Flex 4K shoots up to 1000 fps at 4K; Phantom VEO/Lab > 5000 fps for slow-motion shots. Different from HFR delivery — captured high + played back slow.

**Doug Trumbull** (1942-2022) — *2001: A Space Odyssey* effects, *Close Encounters*, *Blade Runner* (1982), *The Tree of Life*. Inventor of Showscan + Magi (variable frame rate HFR predecessor). Patron saint of HFR.

**Shutter angle** — fraction of one frame period the shutter is open. **180°** = half (= 1/48 s at 24 fps) — produces the canonical cinematic motion blur. **45°-90°** = short — sharp + staccato (the *Saving Private Ryan* + *Gladiator* battle look). **270°-360°** = long — dreamy smear.

**Resolution + frame rate trade-offs**: 8K 60 fps = ~5× the data of 4K 24 fps. Storage + processing + projection bandwidth all scale. Most theatrical infrastructure still 2K-4K 24 fps; HFR remains niche.

question.question: Compute depth of field for a 50 mm T2.0 on Super 35
question.goal: Given $f = 50$ mm, $N = T2.0 \approx f/2$, $c = 0.025$ mm, $u = 2$ m. Find DoF.

steps.prompt: Recall the DoF approximation. Write it.
steps.reveal: $\text{DoF} \approx 2 N c u^2 / f^2$ — valid when $u$ is much less than hyperfocal distance + $u \gg f$.

steps.prompt: Convert all units to mm and substitute. $u = 2000$ mm, $f = 50$ mm, $N = 2$, $c = 0.025$ mm.
Convert to meters. What is the DoF?
steps.reveal: DoF ≈ **160 mm = 0.16 m = 16 cm**. So the in-focus zone is about 8 cm in front of + behind a subject 2 m away. Very shallow — the classical close-up. You will see ear-tip-soft, eye-sharp framing characteristic of T2.0 work.

steps.prompt: How does DoF change if we stop down to T8.0?

acceptedAnswers: increases by factor of 4 to about 64 cm

steps.reveal: Stopping down from T2 to T8 is +4 stops (each stop = $\sqrt{2}$ in $N$, so $\times 4$ in $N$). DoF scales linearly with $N$ → $4 \times 160$ mm = **640 mm ≈ 64 cm**. Now half-meter is in focus — Toland-style deep focus territory.

steps.prompt: Why does anamorphic look 'shallower' than spherical at the same T-stop + framing?

acceptedAnswers: anamorphic squeeze means longer effective focal length for same framing

steps.reveal: Anamorphic 2× compresses horizontally. To frame the same shot you need a longer focal length (~ 2× the horizontal-equivalent). DoF $\propto 1/f^2$ — so anamorphic DoF is shallower for matching framing. Plus oval bokeh + horizontal lens flares give the characteristic anamorphic look.

question.finalResult:
$$\boxed{\text{DoF}_{50\text{mm T2 @ 2m}} \approx 0.16 \text{ m}; \quad \text{DoF}_{50\text{mm T8}} \approx 0.64 \text{ m}}$$

DoF scales linearly with $N$ + inversely with $f^2$. Wide aperture + long focal length + close subject = shallow DoF + isolated subject.

question.question: What is the standard **anamorphic squeeze ratio** + what aesthetic markers does anamorphic produce?
options: 2× horizontal squeeze (compresses a 2.39:1 widescreen into a 4:3 native frame, unsqueezed by projector or post). Visual signatures: **oval / elliptical bokeh** (out-of-focus highlights stretched vertically), **horizontal lens flares** (the J. J. Abrams blue streak), **barrel distortion**, **focus breathing**, and **mumps** (face widening as you focus close). Modern variants include 1.3× + 1.8× for digital. Spherical lenses produce circular bokeh + neutral distortion. Anamorphic is a primary aesthetic decision — Panavision C-Series, G-Series, Cooke Anamorphic/i + Master Anamorphic + Atlas Orion + Hawk are common rental choices.
Anamorphic is a post-only resize, not a lens.
question.explanation: Standard 2× horizontal anamorphic squeeze, producing 2.39:1 widescreen from a 4:3 (or 6:5 native) capture. Aesthetic markers: oval bokeh, horizontal lens flares, barrel distortion, focus breathing, mumps.

slides.workedSolution: Anamorphic = 2× horizontal squeeze, giving 2.39:1 widescreen from a 4:3 native frame. Signatures: oval bokeh, horizontal lens flares, barrel distortion, focus breathing, mumps. Panavision C/G-Series + Cooke Anamorphic/i + Master Anamorphic are typical rentals.

question.question: When does HFR help and when does it hurt?
question.prompt: Doug Trumbull's Showscan (60 fps, 65 mm) and Peter Jackson's *Hobbit* (48 fps) divided audiences — many said the HFR images looked 'like soap operas.' Yet Cameron's *Avatar: The Way of Water* (2022) used HFR successfully. Explain (a) why standard 24 fps + 180° shutter looks 'cinematic'; (b) why high frame rates can break that perception; (c) why Cameron's variable-frame-rate solution worked. Reference Trumbull's psychophysical claims about immersion.

question.question: An Alexa 35 has approximately **17 stops** of dynamic range. Express this as a contrast ratio (linear; $2^{17}$).

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why a 50 mm cinema prime at T1.3 + Alexa 35 + ProRes 4444 is the modern equivalent of Toland's 1941 toolkit — and what the differences mean for working practice.
question.rubric: Mentions: (1) modern cinema prime — Cooke S7/i, Zeiss Supreme, Panavision Primo X — engineered to T1.3-T2.8 wide-open, T-stop calibrated for photometric consistency, neutral colorimetry, low veiling glare; (2) Alexa 35 sensor — 17 stops dynamic range, dual native ISO 800/6400, LogC4 + REVEAL color science; (3) ProRes 4444 codec — broadcast-quality intra-frame compression at 1 GB/min for 4K — manageable file sizes + reliable on-set workflow; (4) by contrast, Toland used 24-28 mm at f/8 + Eastman Super-XX (~ISO 100 push to 200) + arc lighting + slow nitrate negative; (5) modern toolkit allows shooting at much lower light levels with shallower DoF + greater latitude + immediate playback + nondestructive color manipulation in post; (6) tradeoff — film grain + organic highlight roll-off + ritual labor are lost; (7) the choice is now aesthetic + economic, not technical.
